lessons.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Tax Year: Terms to Know Before You Start

body.text: From 1 April 2026, India's income tax runs on a new law with new section numbers and a simpler way of naming years. Your tax rates did not change. What changed is the vocabulary, and if you learn it once now, every advance tax article, challan and notice you meet later will make sense.

children.text: Search online for advance tax and most of what you find still talks about section 234C, "AY 2026-27" and Form 16. None of that is wrong for older years, but it is not the language of the law that governs tax year 2026-27 onwards. This lesson gives you both dictionaries side by side, so you can read old and new sources without getting tangled.
A New Law, Not a New Tax

The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961, which had been amended so many times over six decades that it ran to hundreds of lettered sections such as 80CCD(1B) and 115BAC. Parliament rewrote it in plainer language, folded provisos and explanations into the main text, and replaced long passages with tables and formulas.

stats.label: Schedules
stats.context: More rates and lists moved into schedules

body.text: The Income Tax Department's own FAQ is blunt about this: the 2025 Act does not impose any new tax. Slabs, rates, the ₹10,000 advance tax threshold, the four instalment dates and the 1% monthly interest all carried over. Your existing PAN, and your employer's TAN, also continue unchanged.

children.text: The Tax Year Replaces Two Confusing Terms

markDefs.definition: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the financial year in which income was earned.
Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the year following the previous year, in which that income was assessed and the return filed. Discontinued under the 2025 Act.
The twelve-month financial year beginning 1 April, in which income is earned and on which tax is computed. Defined in section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

children.text: Under the old law, income earned in one year had two labels. The year you earned it was the
, and the following year, when it was assessed, was the
. Generations of first-time taxpayers picked the wrong one on a challan. The 2025 Act replaces both with a single
: the year you earn the income is the year you name.

body.title: Quick Check: Name the Year
body.question: Rohit, a Jaipur-based teacher, sells equity mutual fund units through Groww on 20 January 2027 and makes a capital gain. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, which year does this gain belong to?
body.explanation: January 2027 falls inside the financial year running from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, so the gain belongs to tax year 2026-27. Assessment year is no longer used under the new Act, and tax year 2027-28 only starts on 1 April 2027. Any advance tax on this gain is due by 15 March 2027.

body.label: One exception: a brand-new business or income source
body.value: Tax year starts on the day it begins
body.context: If a business, profession or new source of income starts mid-year, its first tax year runs from that date to 31 March. A freelancer who starts on 1 December 2026 has a first tax year of 1 December 2026 to 31 March 2027.

children.text: Because income earned up to 31 March 2026 stays under the old Act, the months after April 2026 are a genuine overlap. The Income Tax Department's FAQ spells it out: returns for AY 2026-27 are filed on old-Act forms, while advance tax for tax year 2026-27, starting with the June 2026 instalment, follows the new Act. The same person can be dealing with both laws in the same week.

body.title: Scenario: Arjun's Confusing July
body.scenario: It is July 2026. Arjun, a salaried manager in Pune who also earns rent from a flat, is filing his return for the year ended 31 March 2026. A blog post tells him to "check interest under section 234C for AY 2026-27". A second article says "advance tax for tax year 2026-27 is governed by section 408". His friend insists one of them must be outdated, since the old Act has been repealed.
body.prompt: Is either article wrong? Explain what each one applies to, and what Arjun has to do in each case.
body.modelAnswer: Neither is wrong. They refer to two different years. Arjun's return being filed in July 2026 is for income earned from April 2025 to March 2026, which the 1961 Act still governs. For that year, AY 2026-27 is the correct label, section 234C is the correct interest provision, and any balance is paid as self-assessment tax under section 140A. At the same time, his rent for April 2026 onwards belongs to tax year 2026-27 under the 2025 Act. Advance tax on it is governed by sections 403 to 408, and the 15% instalment was already due on 15 June 2026. If he missed it, he should pay the cumulative 45% by 15 September 2026 to limit interest under section 425, the new-Act version of 234C. The repeal of the old Act does not wipe out obligations for years it already governed.

body.text: Before acting on any tax article, notice first which year it talks about. Content published before April 2026 almost always uses 1961 Act section numbers and assessment years. That is fine for FY 2025-26 and earlier, but copying those section numbers into a question about tax year 2026-27 will lead you, and sometimes your CA's junior, to the wrong provision.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: New Section, Old Habit
body.textWithBlank: The interest for missing or short-paying an advance tax instalment, known for decades as section 234C, sits in section ___ of the Income-tax Act, 2025.
body.explanation: Section 425 of the 2025 Act carries forward old section 234C. Its neighbour, section 424, carries forward 234B (interest for not paying or underpaying advance tax), and section 423 carries forward 234A (interest for filing the return late).

body.title: Try It: How Much Shorter?
body.prompt: The 1961 Act had 819 sections and the 2025 Act has 536. By roughly what percentage did the number of sections fall? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: 819 minus 536 is 283 fewer sections. 283 divided by 819 is about 34.6%, or roughly 35%. Prescribed forms fell even faster, from 399 to 190, a drop of about 52%.

children.text: The Income-tax Rules, 2026 renumbered the forms you already know. Their content and purpose are essentially the same, but from tax year 2026-27 your employer and bank will use the new names.

cards.definition: The law that replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961 from 1 April 2026. It rewrote and renumbered the law without imposing any new tax.
The financial year from 1 April to 31 March in which income is earned. Replaces both previous year and assessment year.
Old-Act term for the year in which income was earned. Corresponds to the tax year under the new Act.
Old-Act term for the year after the previous year, when income was assessed. Discontinued under the new Act, but still used for FY 2025-26 and earlier.
Its first tax year runs from the date it starts to the following 31 March.
The new number for Form 16, the salary TDS certificate issued by your employer.
The new number for Form 26AS, the statement of tax credits against your PAN.
The 2025 Act's interest provisions for advance tax, replacing sections 234B and 234C.

points: The Income-tax Act, 2025 came into force on 1 April 2026; it renumbered and simplified the law but imposed no new tax
Tax year replaces both previous year and assessment year: income earned from April 2026 to March 2027 is tax year 2026-27
A business or income source that starts mid-year has a first tax year running from its start date to 31 March
Income up to 31 March 2026 stays under the 1961 Act, so 2026 involves filing old-Act returns while paying new-Act advance tax
Advance tax now sits in sections 403 to 408, with interest in sections 424 and 425
Form 16 is now Form 130 and Form 26AS is now Form 168, with the same purpose as before

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section and form references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026, with the corresponding 1961 Act and 1962 Rules references in brackets or alongside. Provisions reflect the position understood at the time of writing and can change with each Union Budget. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
